messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The gale came without warning three years ago, turning the Atlantic into a churning wall of black water. Kiet was on the bow of the trawler, hauling heavy nets, when the deck pitched violently. He turned to shout to his younger brother, Tien, but a rogue wave swallowed the starboard rail where Tien had been securing a winch. The radio crackled with static before the vessel listed hard. Kiet clawed his way to the wheelhouse, his lungs burning with salt and diesel fumes, while the men below were lost to the sea. He had been on the bridge when the others went under, and that uneven placement became a quiet, unshakable weight in his chest. In the months that followed, the ocean never felt the same. On the water, Kiet worked the winches and mended line with mechanical precision, but his body stayed braced for the next crash. A sudden jolt of the hull would send a jarring tremor through his shoulders; a coiled rope on deck would make his pulse hammer against his ribs as if he were already being dragged under. Nights were worse. He lay awake in his marriage bed, listening to the wind strike the siding, his mind replaying the exact moment the deck tilted. He stopped sleeping through the night, waking instead with a dry mouth and a chest tight with unspoken horror and shame. His quiet certainty that he was fundamentally separate from everyone else, and that people simply could not be trusted to keep the vessel steady, turned every ordinary sound into a physical alarm. Because he believed the world was unsafe and his own survival was an unearned accident, his body reacted to the water, the salt, and the sudden calls of his crew with immediate, violent readiness. The appraisal that he was alone in his guilt had already lit the fuse, so when the diesel engine sputtered or a deckhand laughed too loudly near the rail, his stomach dropped and his breath shallowed instantly, as though the past were pressing against his skin. Over time, the physical toll rewired how he read the world. Every time the hull groaned or a neighbor leaned too close to ask about the catch, Kiet’s heart would kick hard against his sternum, and a cold wave of fear would pool in his gut. That relentless physical alarm taught him what to believe. He began to view his wife’s quiet evenings as distant, as though separated by thick glass, and the constant bodily vigilance convinced him that the past was still happening, that survival was a mistake, and that reaching out would only invite sudden losses. He drifted into a hollow stillness, moving through his routines like a man wading through deep water, while the guilt of living when Tien did not settled heavier on his shoulders. Now, at sixty, Kiet still runs the early morning departures, but he keeps the wheelhouse door shut and avoids the lower deck after dusk. What finally brought him to the clinic was the way his hands shook so badly he dropped a spool of line during Sunday service, followed by a week of waking before dawn with his throat tight and his mind braced for a storm that never broke. He told his wife he was coming for answers, though his real fear was that the water would never stop rising. He hoped, quietly, to find a way to step back onto solid ground without feeling like a fraud for still being here.
